section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Pick the right suvat in two seconds
body:
Write the five letters $s,u,v,a,t$; tick the three you know and the one you want; pick the equation that **lacks the fifth**.

| Missing | Use |
|---|---|
| $s$ | $v=u+at$ |
| $v$ | $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$ |
| $a$ | $s=\tfrac12(u+v)t$ |
| $t$ | $v^2=u^2+2as$ |
| $u$ | $s=vt-\tfrac12at^2$ |

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Average velocity trick
body: For constant acceleration, average velocity is $\tfrac12(u+v)$, so $s=\tfrac12(u+v)t$. A particle slows from $20$ to $0$ in $5\ \mathrm s$: $s=\tfrac12(20)(5)=50\ \mathrm m$, no $a$ needed.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Vertical motion is symmetric
body: Thrown up at $u$: time to top $=\dfrac ug$, max height $=\dfrac{u^2}{2g}$, **same speed at the same height going up and down**, total flight time (back to start) $=\dfrac{2u}g$. Landing speed from height $h$ (dropped) $=\sqrt{2gh}$.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Choose "up" as positive and keep $a=-g$
body: A single equation covers the whole flight. A quadratic in $t$ gives two times: the up-pass and the down-pass.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Successive equal intervals from rest
body: Distances covered in successive equal times are in the ratio $1:3:5:7:\dots$ And $s\propto t^2$.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Distance in the $n$th second
body: $s_n=u+a\left(n-\tfrac12\right)$ (velocity at the **midpoint** of that second). Difference of distances in consecutive equal intervals $T$: $\Delta s=aT^2$ — find $a$ from two distances with no $u$.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Accelerate then decelerate over a fixed distance
body: From rest to rest in distance $s$, accelerating at $a$ then decelerating at $b$: top speed $V^2=\dfrac{2s\,ab}{a+b}$, total time $T=\sqrt{\dfrac{2s(a+b)}{ab}}$. Check with $a=b$: $V^2=sa$, $T=2\sqrt{s/a}$ ✓.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: v–t graph: area $=$ displacement, gradient $=$ acceleration
body: Break the area into triangles and rectangles; a trapezium is $\tfrac12(a+b)h$. **Total distance** counts areas below the axis as positive.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Trapezium shortcut for a three-stage journey
body: Times $t_1,t_2,t_3$ with top speed $V$: distance $=\tfrac12V(T+t_2)$ where $T$ is total time and $t_2$ the constant-speed time (area of a trapezium: $\tfrac12(\text{parallel sides})\times V$).

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Average speed
body: $=\dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$, **not** the mean of speeds. Two equal distances at $v_1,v_2$: $\dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1+v_2}$ (harmonic mean).

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Meeting and chase
body: Write both displacements from a common origin and time-zero, then equate: $s_1(t)=s_2(t)$. If one starts later by $T$, use $(t-T)$. Meeting while moving in opposite directions: **sum of distances** = initial gap; same direction: **difference** = initial gap.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Relative velocity
body: For two bodies moving along a line, relative speed $=|v_1-v_2|$ (same direction) or $v_1+v_2$ (towards each other). Time to catch up $=\dfrac{\text{gap}}{\text{relative speed}}$ — no equations of motion needed.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Stopping distance
body: $\dfrac{u^2}{2a}$; doubling speed quadruples it. Reaction time adds $u\times t_r$.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Dropped and thrown at the same time
body: Relative acceleration is zero, so the gap between them changes at constant rate $u_1-u_2$.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Check units and signs
body: A positive $s$ with negative $v$ at the end means "gone up then fallen back past its start": fine. A negative time is rejected.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: $v=\dfrac{ds}{dt}$, $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$; integrate back with a constant
body: Use the starting condition ($t=0$, known $s$ or $v$) immediately to fix the constant.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Maximum or minimum speed
body: when $a=0$ (but check the endpoints).

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Displacement vs distance
body: if the particle turns round, split at $v=0$ and add the magnitudes.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Particle at rest
body:
means $v=0$; **instantaneous** at a given time means substitute; **returns to start** means $s=0$ again.
- **Power rule in time:** $\int t^n=\dfrac{t^{n+1}}{n+1}$; **definite** integral $\int_{t_1}^{t_2}v\,dt$ gives displacement.

title: Position of a body with constant velocity
body: $\mathbf r=\mathbf r_0+\mathbf vt$ . Two bodies meet when $\mathbf r_A=\mathbf r_B$ **at the same $t$**: equate the $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ parts and check both give the same $t$. If the times differ, they only cross paths.

title: Closest approach
body: Relative position $\mathbf d(t)=\mathbf d_0+\mathbf vt$ where $\mathbf v$ is the relative velocity. Minimise $|\mathbf d|^2$: $t=-\dfrac{\mathbf d_0\cdot\mathbf v}{|\mathbf v|^2}$, and the least distance is $\dfrac{|d_{0x}v_y-d_{0y}v_x|}{|\mathbf v|}$. Quicker than differentiating a quadratic.

title: Speed and bearing
body: Speed $=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ for $a\mathbf i+b\mathbf j$. Direction angle from east $\theta=\tan^{-1}\dfrac ba$ (adjust quadrant). **Bearing $=90^\circ-\theta$** (mod $360^\circ$), north is $000^\circ$.

title: Unit vector
body: $\hat{\mathbf a}=\dfrac{\mathbf a}{|\mathbf a|}$. Vector of given magnitude $k$ in the direction of $\mathbf a$: $k\hat{\mathbf a}$.

title: Parallel vectors
body: $\mathbf a=\lambda\mathbf b$, so $\dfrac{a_x}{b_x}=\dfrac{a_y}{b_y}$. **"Moving parallel to $\mathbf i+2\mathbf j$"**: components in ratio $1:2$.

title: Distance between two position vectors
body: $|\mathbf a-\mathbf b|$. Midpoint: $\dfrac{\mathbf a+\mathbf b}2$.

title: Pythagorean angle triples
body: $3\!:\!4\!:\!5$, $5\!:\!12\!:\!13$, $8\!:\!15\!:\!17$, $7\!:\!24\!:\!25$ let you replace $\cos\theta,\sin\theta$ by fractions without a calculator. "$\tan\theta=\tfrac34$" means $\sin\theta=\tfrac35$, $\cos\theta=\tfrac45$.

title: Resolve into components
body: force $F$ at angle $\theta$ to a direction has component $F\cos\theta$ along it and $F\sin\theta$ perpendicular. **Pick the angle to the axis you resolve along**, and sketch to check whether it's $\cos$ or $\sin$.

title: Resultant of two forces at angle $\theta$
body: (beyond spec): $R=\sqrt{F_1^2+F_2^2+2F_1F_2\cos\theta}$, and its angle with $F_1$ is $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{F_2\sin\theta}{F_1+F_2\cos\theta}$. Right angles: just Pythagoras.

title: Constant velocity change
body: $\mathbf v=\mathbf u+\mathbf at$ works component by component, and so do all suvat equations (not $v^2=u^2+2as$ in vector form unless you use dot products).

title: Newton's second law in vectors
body: $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$, so $\mathbf a=\dfrac{\mathbf F}m$ and velocity after $t$ is $\mathbf u+\dfrac{\mathbf F}mt$.

title: Lami's theorem (beyond spec)
body: three forces in equilibrium: $\dfrac{F_1}{\sin\alpha}=\dfrac{F_2}{\sin\beta}=\dfrac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$ where $\alpha$ is the angle between $F_2$ and $F_3$ (opposite $F_1$). One line for a three-force triangle.

title: Triangle of forces
body: three forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle: use sine/cosine rules.

title: Write $F=ma$ along the motion and equilibrium across it
body: Resolve **in the direction of acceleration** (forces helping $-$ forces opposing $=ma$), and **perpendicular** with no acceleration (they balance).

title: Connected particles: treat the whole system first
body: For two particles joined by a string moving together, $F_{\text{net}}=(m_1+m_2)a$ gives $a$ immediately; then use **one** particle to find the tension. Internal tensions cancel.

title: Pulley over a smooth peg (hanging masses $m_1<m_2$)
body:
$$a=\frac{(m_2-m_1)g}{m_1+m_2},\qquad T=\frac{2m_1m_2g}{m_1+m_2}.$$
Check: $m_1=m_2\Rightarrow a=0$, $T=mg$ ✓.

title: Particle on a smooth table pulled by a hanging mass
body: $a=\dfrac{m_2g}{m_1+m_2}$, $T=\dfrac{m_1m_2g}{m_1+m_2}$. With friction $\mu$ on the table: $a=\dfrac{m_2g-\mu m_1g}{m_1+m_2}$.

title: Rough slope
body: Resolve perpendicular: $R=mg\cos\theta$. Down the slope $a=g(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)$. **Equilibrium on the point of slipping:** $\tan\theta=\mu$ (angle of friction). The coefficient $\mu=\tan\theta$ is a one-line "find $\mu$" question.

title: Smooth slope
body: $a=g\sin\theta$ regardless of the mass. Speed at the bottom of a smooth slope of height $h$ is $\sqrt{2gh}$ whatever the slope angle.

title: Friction: $F\le\mu R$, equality only in limiting equilibrium or while sliding
body: Static and not about to slip: $F$ equals whatever balances the other forces. **Always find $R$ first**, and remember a vertical component of the applied force changes $R$: pulling up at angle $\alpha$: $R=mg-P\sin\alpha$; pushing down: $R=mg+P\sin\alpha$.

title: Best angle to pull a block (beyond spec)
body: Minimum pulling force to move a block of weight $W$ on rough ground is at $\tan\alpha=\mu$: $P_{\min}=\dfrac{\mu W}{\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}$.

title: Lifts (apparent weight)
body: Lift accelerating **upwards** at $a$: reaction $R=m(g+a)$; downwards: $R=m(g-a)$. Free fall: $R=0$ ("weightless").

title: String goes slack
body: When a hanging mass hits the floor, tension disappears: the other particle then decelerates (rough table) or moves at constant velocity (smooth). Find the speed at the moment of impact with suvat, then restart $F=ma$.

title: Tension in a string over a pulley is the same on both sides
body: (light string, smooth pulley). A **light** rod or string has no mass, so the two end forces are equal.

title: Two-pulley/inclined plus hanging mass
body: write $F=ma$ **for each particle with a consistent positive direction along the string**, then add the equations to eliminate $T$.

title: Constant force from a velocity change
body: $F=\dfrac{m(v-u)}t$ (impulse–momentum). **Impulse $=Ft=mv-mu$** (vector; sign the directions).

title: Collisions (momentum conserved)
body: $m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2$. Coalescing: $v=\dfrac{m_1u_1+m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$. **Direction of an unknown velocity: assume positive and let the sign speak.**

title: Restitution (beyond spec)
body: speed of separation $=e\times$ speed of approach.

title: Work–energy (beyond spec)
body: $\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mu^2=$ net work. Great when the path is not straight and time doesn't matter: $v^2=u^2+2gh$ for a free fall of height $h$ regardless of the path on a smooth surface.

title: Power (beyond spec)
body: $P=Fv$; at maximum speed driving force $=$ resistance.

title: Moments around the point that kills unknowns
body: Take moments about the pivot where the unknown force acts, so its moment is zero. Moment $=$ force $\times$ **perpendicular** distance.

title: Equilibrium: three equations
body: Forces vertically, forces horizontally, moments about a point; **use the one that isolates the unknown**.

title: Tilting condition
body: A beam is about to tilt about a support when the **reaction at the other support is zero**. Put $R=0$ and take moments about the pivot.

title: Uniform beam
body: weight acts at the **midpoint** . A non-uniform one: weight at the centre of mass (given distance).

title: Ladder problems
body: Moments about the foot (kills friction and normal reaction there), vertical balance for friction with the ground: $F=\mu R$ at limiting equilibrium; the wall reaction is horizontal if the wall is smooth.

title: Beam with a person or particle walking
body: Find the extreme position by letting a reaction $\to0$: gives the greatest distance before tilting.

title: Equal and opposite moment checks
body: clockwise moments $=$ anticlockwise moments. If you get a negative reaction you've chosen the wrong direction or the beam has tilted.

title: Centre of mass of two masses
body: $\bar x=\dfrac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}$ — equivalent to moments about the origin.

title: "Light"
body:
= mass negligible so tension is equal throughout. **"Smooth"** = no friction. **"Inextensible"** = same acceleration magnitude along the string. **"Particle"** = no size, no rotation. **"Uniform"** = mass evenly distributed so weight is at the midpoint. **"Rough"** = friction present.
- **Modelling assumptions answer:** one clear sentence. "Air resistance is negligible", "the rod is rigid", "the string doesn't stretch", "the pulley is smooth so the tension is the same on both sides", "$g$ is constant".

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Reset the clock when the motion changes
source: Pearson WME01 Jan 2024 examiner report Q8(b)
body: At an impact, break, or change of surface, record the current position and velocity, then start the next phase at local time $\tau=0$. Recalculate $a$ for that phase; one suvat equation across the boundary works only if acceleration stays constant.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Screen a meeting quadratic before solving
body: If equating two positions produces $At^2+Bt+C=0$ with $A\ne0$, the discriminant $B^2-4AC$ tells you whether there are zero, one, or two real candidate meetings. Keep only nonnegative roots inside the time interval where both position formulae apply, and substitute back.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Time spent above a height
body: For a vertical projection at speed $u$, solving $h=ut-\tfrac12gt^2$ gives the duration above height $h$ as $2\sqrt{u^2-2gh}/g$ when $0\le h\le u^2/(2g)$. It becomes zero at the maximum height, which checks the result.

section: 1. Kinematics in a straight line (suvat and graphs)
title: Distinguish a velocity graph from a speed graph
source: Pearson WME01 Jan 2024 examiner report Q6(d)
body: With up positive, vertical velocity is the straight line $v=u-gt$, while speed is $|u-gt|$ and has a V-shaped graph. Reflect the negative part only for speed or total distance; check that the descending velocity still has gradient $-g$.

title: Name the axis in a direction answer
source: Pearson WME01 Jun 2023 examiner report Q2(b)
body: After finding an angle from vector components, write, for example, "$\theta$ above the positive $\mathbf i$ direction" and use the component signs to choose the quadrant. A bare $\tan^{-1}(y/x)$ can give the wrong direction when $x<0$.

title: Compare squared distances
body: If a question asks whether the least separation exceeds a nonnegative threshold $r$, compare $d_{\min}^2$ with $r^2$ and skip the final square root. Check that the calculated closest-approach time lies in the allowed interval; otherwise use its nearest endpoint.

title: Use the force diagram as an equation checklist
source: Pearson WME01 Jun 2023 examiner report Q7
body: For each body, draw and label only forces acting on that body, then tick each arrow as it enters the appropriate $F=ma$ equation. Check that the mass multiplying $a$ belongs to the same body and that no weight or tension was silently omitted.

title: Recalculate the normal reaction for oblique forces
source: Cambridge 9709 Jun 2024 examiner report Paper 42 Q5
body: If a tension $T$ pulls at angle $\phi$ above a plane inclined at $\theta$, $R=mg\cos\theta-T\sin\phi$ while contact remains. Check $R\ge0$ and use this value, rather than $mg\cos\theta$, in any friction limit.

title: Reverse friction after a turn
source: Pearson WME01 Jan 2024 examiner report Q8(b)
body: On a rough surface, label the actual direction of motion in each phase and make kinetic friction oppose it. After a reversal, form a new force equation; check that friction's arrow has reversed too.

title: Find required friction before testing the limit
body: In equilibrium, solve the along-surface balance for signed $F_{\rm req}$, then test $|F_{\rm req}|\le\mu R$. Its sign gives the friction direction, and equality identifies the limiting case.

title: One string distance can mean different vertical changes
source: Cambridge 9709 Jun 2024 examiner report Paper 42 Q7(b)
body: With a taut, inextensible string, if one particle rises $x$ vertically while another moves $x$ along a plane at $\theta$, their vertical changes are $x$ and $x\sin\theta$. For a vertical gap $H$ closing between them, check the geometry with $x+x\sin\theta=H$ before using suvat.

title: Choose the body with known velocities for impulse
source: Pearson WME01 Jun 2023 examiner report Q1(c)
body: When impulse on a particle is requested, use $\mathbf J=m(\mathbf v-\mathbf u)$ for the particle whose before and after velocities are given. Check that a requested magnitude is nonnegative and has units $\mathrm{N\,s}$ or $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

title: Separate mass from weight in the data margin
source: Pearson WME01 Jun 2023 examiner report Q6
body: Mark a given $m\,\mathrm{kg}$ as mass and $W\,\mathrm N$ as an already calculated weight; only the first needs multiplication by $g$. Check every force equation is in newtons, preventing an erroneous $Wg$.

title: Treat two support reactions as load shares
body: For vertical loads on a horizontal beam supported at $x=0,L$, let $W=\sum W_i$ and $\bar x=\sum W_ix_i/W$; then $R_L=W\bar x/L$ and $R_0=W-R_L$. Check $R_0+R_L=W$ and both reactions are nonnegative while both supports touch.

title: Cancel $g$ only after writing every weight moment
body: When every term in a moments equation is a weight $m_i g$ times a distance, write those terms first and divide the entire equation by $g$. Check that no independent force in newtons was included before cancellation.

title: Locate the tipping boundary from the load centre
body: With only vertical loads and upward supports, the weighted position $\bar x=\sum W_ix_i/\sum W_i$ must lie between the supports for both reactions to be nonnegative. At either support position the opposite reaction is zero, which checks a tilting calculation.

title: Keep exact trigonometric ratios until the end
source: Cambridge 9709 Jun 2024 examiner report Paper 42 Q4
body: If $\tan\theta=p/q$, use a right triangle to keep $\sin\theta=p/\sqrt{p^2+q^2}$ and $\cos\theta=q/\sqrt{p^2+q^2}$ rather than rounding $\theta$ first. Check the final numerical answer with the paper's required significant figures.

title: A coefficient of friction may exceed one
body:
Since $\mu=F_{\max}/R$ is a force ratio, a calculated $\mu>1$ is not automatically impossible. Substitute it into the limiting-friction and force equations instead of treating it like a probability. [src: Pearson 9MA0-32 Jun 2024 examiner report Q7(b)]

# S1 Statistics
